title: An Evening Stroll
premise: A quiet circuit of the familiar streets: a shopfront, the corner where the town's newspaper began and two public houses, with nothing to count or carry.

opening.text:
JAUNT: AN EVENING STROLL. Dusk on 1 July 1835. The land buyers have gone in to supper, the river has gone quiet, and for once there is nothing you need to do. Chicago is not two years old as a town: when it was incorporated in August 1833, only 'thirteen votes were cast by the twenty-eight legal electors'. Now strangers arrive by the boatload.

Take a slow circuit of the familiar streets: from the Sauganash, past the village's first frame store and the corner where its first newspaper was printed, to the hotel where the town holds its meetings. Then decide where the evening ends.

stops.text: Begin at the Sauganash, on the corner of Lake and Market above the South Branch, white and two-storey with bright-blue shutters and newly fitted up this June. Mark Beaubien built it, and he has had a busy time in this town. Moses and Kirkland call him 'the fun of every funeral and the life of every wake', and list him 'As fiddler, landlord, merchant, ferryman and a patron of horse racing'. In May 1833 Father St. Cyr 'celebrated his first mass in a log cabin belonging to Mark Beaubien'.
stops.narrative: Set out from a public house's door.

stops.text: Over to the river and east along South Water Street to LaSalle and P. F. W. Peck's store, the first two-storey frame in the village, built of lumber 'sawed from black walnut trees'. Peck sells dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots, shoes and hats, and he is a careful man. Years from now he will be credited 'with having $40,000 in cash locked in an iron safe in his dwelling', and thought 'nearly as wealthy as John Jacob Astor'.
stops.narrative: A shopfront on the trading street.

stops.text: One block east, at South Water and Clark, John Calhoun began printing the Chicago Democrat in 1833; by 20 May its office was over Jones & King's hardware along the street. It comes out on Wednesdays, and today's is No. 11 of its second volume. When the mail comes in, the town has another way to get the news: 'some one with a good voice would mount a dry goods box' and read it out, and if politics ran high, there were two boxes and two readers.

South to Lake Street and west to Wells, and the Exchange Coffee House, another house Mark Beaubien built, kept as a hotel since August 1834 by Mr. and Mrs. Murphy. The town's Democrats met here in April and again in June to choose their candidates, and a dancing master took his pupils' addresses here last winter. Choose where the evening ends.

choices.label: End at the Exchange
choices.consequence: Finish the circuit at the Murphys' corner of Lake and Wells.

choices.label: Walk back to the Sauganash
choices.consequence: West along Lake Street to the door you set out from.

stops.narrative: A second public house, and a choice of where to stop.

legs.note: North from the Market Street corner to the river and east along South Water Street to LaSalle, about 0.35 km.
legs.story: From the public house to the trading street, as the shutters close.

legs.note: One block east along South Water Street, from LaSalle to Clark.
legs.story: A few doors on, to the printer's first corner.

legs.note: South on Clark to Lake Street and west to the Wells Street corner, about 0.25 km.
legs.story: Turn back toward the evening's end.

endings.text: You end the stroll at the corner of Lake and Wells in the last of the light, having passed the village's first frame store, its first newspaper's corner and two of Mark Beaubien's houses. Not bad for a town that is not two years old.
You walk back west along Lake Street to the Sauganash and close the circuit where it began. If the windows are open, you may hear the fiddle.

keepsake.title: A Pleasant Circuit
keepsake.text: A fictional note of a quiet evening's walk past a store, a printing office's first corner and two public houses.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun describes the Sauganash in 1831 as 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters'.
evidence.locator: Ch. XVII, 'Chicago in 1831' — the Wolf Point houses, Mark Beaubien's house just completed.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town's public houses (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Sauganash stood at the south-east corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east bank of the South Branch.
evidence.reasoning: The corner is given by the hotel chronology and the Chicago Landmark designation; the building's coordinate in the scene is the structure record's platted-corner derivation and carries the georeference's uncertainty of about 20 m.

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats.
evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck’s standing card, run to 10 Dec 1834); 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4 (‘a full stock of fresh GOODS’). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Peck's store stood at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle Streets; the corner is documented and the footprint's coordinate is derived.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the corner. The structure record derives the coordinate from the modern West Wacker Drive / LaSalle intersection with a working uncertainty of about 20 m, so the stop calls the footprint our placement.

evidence.text: The Democrat’s first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun’s office.

evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat’s colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King’s hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.
evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Democrat came out once a week, on Wednesdays, and the number dated 1 July 1835 is No. 11 of its second volume.
evidence.reasoning: Read off the issue numbers this project already cites from the same transcription: 20 May 1835 is Vol. II No. 5, 27 May No. 6, 10 June No. 8, 24 June No. 10 and 1 July No. 11. The numbers advance by one for every seven days, and 1 July 1835 fell on a Wednesday, so each of those dates is a Wednesday. No masthead statement of the paper's terms or day of issue has been read for this claim.

evidence.text: Mark Beaubien built a new house on the north-west corner of Wells and Lake streets; in August 1834 Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of it as a hotel, christened it the Exchange Coffee House, and remained until 1836.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 633, the hotel chapter; the life of Mark Beaubien; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Exchange Coffee House entry.

evidence.text: When the town was incorporated in August 1833, 'thirteen votes were cast by the twenty-eight legal electors', twelve in favour and one, Russel E. Heacock's, against.
evidence.locator: p. 91, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12319-12325 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland call Mark Beaubien 'the jovial, generous Frenchman', 'the fun of every funeral and the life of every wake'; 'As fiddler, landlord, merchant, ferryman and a patron of horse racing he was alike interesting and always original.'
evidence.locator: p. 560, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98698-98710 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Father John M. I. St. Cyr 'celebrated his first mass in a log cabin belonging to Mark Beaubien, May 5, 1833'.
evidence.locator: p. 92, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12519-12525 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck's two-storey frame store, the first in the village, was built of lumber 'sawed from black walnut trees' and 'brought from Detroit by a boat'; his goods moved into it in the fall of 1831.
evidence.locator: p. 570, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 99826-99842 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1835 Peck joined the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company and married Mary K. Wythe of Philadelphia; years later he was credited 'with having $40,000 in cash locked in an iron safe in his dwelling, and was considered nearly as wealthy as John Jacob Astor'.
evidence.locator: p. 571, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 99877-99917 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: When the mail came, 'often irregular and long delayed', the town gathered at the post office, where 'some one with a good voice would mount a dry goods box' and read the news from Washington and New York; 'If politics ran high, two dry-goods boxes and two readers of opposite parties would be utilized.'
evidence.locator: p. 99-100, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13378-13395 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat reports a large meeting of the town's Democrats held at the Exchange Coffee House in April 1835, and in June 1835 a meeting of the Democratic party held there to nominate candidates for the coming town election.
evidence.locator: 20 May 1835, p. 1, col. 3, 'Great Democratic Meeting', the meeting dated April 1835 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_05_20#c001); 10 June 1835, p. 2, col. 5, 'Town Election', held '[Satu]rday evening last' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c002). Transcription-mediated readings of interleaved columns; the April day and weekday as transcribed do not agree, so the stop gives the month only.

evidence.text: J. A. Marshall's notice of a dancing school, dated 19 November 1834, asked those wishing to become pupils to leave their address at the Exchange Coffee House.
evidence.locator: 19 Nov 1834, p. 3, col. 2, the card headed 'DANCING.' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1834_11_19#c004). Transcription-mediated reading of an interleaved column.

evidence.text: The evening, the stroll, the route order, the looking from the street, the choice of where to end, both endings and the A Pleasant Circuit keepsake are invented connective narrative. The evening changes no lighting in the scene; no entertainment, meeting, purchase or dated event is claimed for it, no interior is opened and no one is met.
